title: The particle model and density
keyIdea: The arrangement, movement and spacing of particles explain density, squashing, flowing and changes of state.

kid: The particle model explains things using particles. In a solid, particles are close and fixed. In a liquid they are close but move around. In a gas they are spread out.
Density is how much mass is packed into a space. Most solids are dense, because their particles are packed closely. Gases have a low density, because their particles are far apart.
adult: Density = mass ÷ volume, often in g/cm³. A 20 cm³ block with a mass of 54 g has a density of 54 ÷ 20 = 2.7 g/cm³. A change of state changes the spacing, so it changes the density. The mass stays the same.
Every model has limits. Real particles are not hard little balls. Simple diagrams also leave out the forces between them. Even so, the model predicts a lot.

familyTip: Weigh a full glass of water, then work out its density using the volume printed on a measuring jug.

practice.prompt: A block has a mass of 54 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
An object has a mass of {=d*v} g and a volume of {v} cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
Why is steam much less dense than liquid water?
choices: The same particles are much more spread out
practice.explain: The particles are identical, but in steam they are far apart, so less mass fits in each cm³.

practice.prompt: A liquid has a density of {d} g/cm³. What is the mass of {v} cm³ of it, in g?
When water boils, what is overcome?
choices: The bonds inside each water particle
Nothing: the particles just get bigger
practice.hint: Boiling doesn't make a new substance.
practice.explain: Boiling overcomes the forces between particles. Each water particle stays whole.

pool.prompt: A stone has a mass of {=d*v} g and a volume of {v} cm³. Find its density in g/cm³.
A metal has a density of {d} g/cm³. What is the mass of {v} cm³ of it, in g?
Which is best explained by particles being far apart?
pool.explain: Gases squash because there is space between their particles.

pool.prompt: 100 g of ice melts. What is the mass of the water?
pool.explain: Still 100 g. The same particles are just arranged differently.

pool.prompt: Which is a limit of the simple particle model?
choices: It shows particles as hard balls, which they are not
It says gases have no particles
pool.hint: What do the diagrams leave out?
pool.explain: Real particles aren't hard spheres, and the diagrams don't show the forces between them.

pool.prompt: The gas in a balloon is cooled. Its particles…
choices: slow down, and the balloon shrinks
pool.explain: The particles slow down and hit the walls less, so the balloon shrinks. The particles stay the same size.

pool.prompt: Usually, which state of a substance has the highest density?
pool.explain: Usually the solid. Water is a famous exception: ice floats because it is less dense than water.

visual.caption: Same particles, same mass: watch how much space they take up as the state changes.
